1:
Why a blessing follows the song they explain by contrast. Henry says that in the foregoing chapter Moses had thundered out the terrors of the Lord, a chapter like Ezekiel's roll, full of lamentation and mourning and woe, and now subjoins a blessing to soften it, that he might not seem to part in anger, leaving his peace to rest on all the sons of peace among them; and he observes that Christ's last work on earth was likewise to bless his disciples, parting as friends. Calvin gives the relation another figure, the bitterness of the song seasoned by this blessing as if by sugar, and says Moses left a testimony of God's perpetual grace, depositing an inestimable treasure in the people's hands, being as it were their second father, ratifying the covenant anew lest its memory be lost. Ellicott quotes Rashi on the words before his death: if not then, when should he?

The title man of God Ellicott says is here used for the first time, its counterpart standing in the next chapter, where Moses the servant of Jehovah died; and he draws the rule that the more a man is servant to Jehovah, the more is he a man of Elohim to his fellows; after Moses it is Elijah and Elisha who are so described. Gill reports that it is a title given to prophets, that Onkelos paraphrases it Moses the prophet of the Lord, and that Aben Ezra takes it as showing he blessed Israel by a spirit of prophecy on his last day. Wesley makes the point practically, that the title acquaints them that the prophecies following were no inventions of his but divine inspirations, and adds what the others pass over, that Simeon alone is omitted, either in detestation of that parent's bloody carriage, for which Jacob gave a curse rather than a blessing, or because the tribe had no distinct inheritance but its portion inside Judah.

Keil sets the two blessings side by side as a test. If the blessings of these two men of God have really been preserved to us, he says, and are not later inventions, we should expect their contents to be essentially the same, the blessing of Moses simply confirming the dying patriarch's and founded upon it; this is most conspicuous in the blessing upon Joseph, and unmistakeable in several others, though Moses is not surpassed by Jacob in independence or originality. On the theophany Ellicott reads a sunrise: the light rose from Sinai, the tops of the hills of Seir caught its rays, and the full blaze shone on Paran. Wesley harmonises the three places as stages of one journey, beginning at Sinai where the first appearance was and going on to Seir and Paran, whence God led them toward the promised land and appeared gloriously in subduing Sihon and Og.

Two words in the second verse Ellicott and Calvin will not let stand. Ellicott says that he came with ten thousands of saints is a mere mistranslation, the preposition being from and not with; Calvin objects to another rendering, that some translate improperly, God comes to Sinai, whereas Moses means he came from thence, when his brightness was made manifest. Whom he loved divides them three ways. Keil renders it, yea, nations he loves, insisting that the peoples here are not the tribes of Israel at all. Calvin states the Gentile reading and rejects it, holding it more correct to refer the word only to the children of Abraham, called peoples because, from the multitude into which their several tribes had grown, they might be reckoned as so many nations. Ellicott takes them for all who should hereafter become his people. Clarke and Wesley keep to Israel, Wesley adding that the change between his and thy is frequent in Hebrew, and Gill that the word for loving means embracing in the arms and bosom.
4:
Who was king in Jeshurun they answer two ways, and Gill takes both. Either God, as Jarchi holds, since the government was a theocracy and their laws came immediately from him, so that when they were importunate for a king they are said to have rejected the Lord from reigning; or Moses, as Aben Ezra and Maimonides hold, who under God had the civil government. Wesley takes the second, that Moses was their king not in title but in reality, under God their supreme governor and lawgiver, owned as such whenever princes and people met for public affairs. Keil refers the clause to God, who became King in Jeshurun, having given the law through Moses to Jacob's congregation as a precious possession. Calvin sees a claim: Moses applies what he had declared of God's glory and the Law's excellency to his own person, boasting that he was appointed teacher of the people not for a brief period but for all ages, and claiming the royal supremacy, not because he had ruled after the manner of kings but that the office's dignity might add weight.

Why the law is called an inheritance Wesley and Calvin explain differently. Wesley says its obligation was hereditary, passing from parents to children, and was besides the best part of their inheritance, the greatest gift God bestowed on them; Calvin finds in the same word the perpetuity of the Law. Wesley adds that Moses speaks of himself here in the third person, as is very usual in Hebrew. Gill keeps the authorship clear on both sides: the law was of God, of his enacting, a declaration of his will with his authority stamped on it; but it was delivered to Moses and by him to Israel, on whom he urged obedience, so that it is said to come by him and is sometimes called the law of Moses.

That Reuben is blessed first, having lost the birthright, Henry makes a rule: we should not insult over the disgraced, nor desire to perpetuate marks of infamy upon any, though ever so justly fastened at first. Clarke explains the doubled form from Ainsworth, that Scripture usually sets down things of importance by affirming one part and denying the other, as in thou shalt die and not live, and I shall not die but live. The ancient versions, however, take the two clauses of two worlds. Wesley reports that all the ancient paraphrasts refer this to the other world, so far were they from expecting temporal blessings only: Onkelos has, let Reuben live in life eternal and not die the second death, while Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum have, let him live in this world and not die the death the wicked die in the world to come. Gill notes the same of all three Targums, Ellicott quoting Rashi to like effect.

The clause about Reuben's numbers both find hard, and the Greek settles it by force. Keil says the words have been explained in very different ways and the noun here cannot bear its usual sense; Ellicott calls the sentence difficult and reports that the Septuagint simply inserts Simeon, let Simeon be many in number, judging the insertion unnecessary. Of Judah, Calvin meets the objection that some abatement seems made from the splendid blessings Jacob had promised, and denies it: the decree of Judah's supremacy is unaltered, and Moses merely reminds them how difficult its accomplishment would be. Keil places Judah before Levi as the royal tribe, from whom the sceptre was not to depart. Ellicott hears a kingly blessing, so that thinking of the Lion of the tribe of Judah we say, thy kingdom come, and follows Rashi in counting the prayers heard from Judah's lips, those of David and Solomon, of Asa and Jehoshaphat, of Hezekiah against Sennacherib, down to the last line of Old Testament history, a prayer of Judah by Nehemiah's mouth.
8:
Why Levi is treated at such length Ellicott and Henry flatly contradict each other. Ellicott says that, next to Joseph, this tribe has the largest share in Moses' last words, as we might expect, it being his own; Henry says the opposite, that Moses expresses himself at large not so much because it was his own tribe, for he takes no notice of his relation to it, as because it was God's. Who the holy one is they also divide upon. Clarke takes it of Aaron, whose office was the most holy man could hold, and the more so as he was the type of Jesus, from whom Urim, all light and wisdom, and Thummim, all excellence and perfection, are derived. Henry agrees, adding that Holiness to the Lord was written on the forehead in token of it. Ellicott splits the reference, letting Massah point back to Aaron and the renouncing of kindred forward to Eleazar or Phinehas; Wesley reads it as settling the priesthood in Aaron's family.

Keil makes the whole a prayer to God, rendering it, thy right and thy light is to thy godly man, and says Levi proved itself a holy one although in the latter trial Moses and Aaron themselves stumbled, the Levites having risen in defence of the honour of the Lord. Henry hears there an acknowledgment that God might justly have displaced Aaron and his seed for the sin at Meribah. Who said unto his father Clarke approaches by listing the proposals and refusing most: some think the words spoken of the tribe of Levi, others of all the tribes, others of the Messiah, but several interpretations founded on these suppositions are too recondite to be resorted to till a plain literal sense is made out, and he supposes the whole spoken of Aaron and his tribe, the law forbidding the high priest to mourn even for father, mother, brother or child.

Gill offers two senses, either the high priests not defiling themselves for the dead, or rather their having no respect to relations in judgment, determining every cause by the law impartially. Keil refers them to the day the Levites drew the sword at Sinai, and Wesley likewise, adding that when the rest broke covenant by the calf that tribe kept itself pure. Calvin reads the whole blessing as a deliberate modification of an older sentence: Jacob had called Simeon and Levi brethren, instruments of cruelty in their habitations, and had refused to come into their secret; their descendants might well have been discouraged when the founder of their race had thus abominated them, and Moses' qualification of that harsher sentence was made not only for the tribe's sake but rather for the whole people's.

In Aaron, Calvin adds, an example is set before all the Levites: he renounced his own flesh and blood that he might be the more disencumbered for obeying God, and all pastors must likewise put off the earthly affections which would otherwise keep them from devoting themselves entirely to him. The prayer for Levi's substance they explain from his landlessness, two of them finding its answer in the Maccabees. Ellicott says a blessing on his substance means a blessing to the whole land, Levi's substance being Israel's tithe, and the chief work of his hands mediatorial for all Israel; on the prayer against those that rise up he follows Rashi to the great war begun by the Asmonaeans, Mattathias the father of the Maccabees having been a priest of the sons of Joiarib. Gill reports Jarchi to the same effect, and that some render substance as a host or army, their service being a warfare. Clarke argues economically, that the more fruitful the land the more abundant the tithes; Calvin says the supplication tacitly provides against the poverty awaiting them; Wesley, that Moses prayed so earnestly because men who must teach and reprove would have many enemies.
12:
Why Benjamin stands where he does they explain by geography and history. Gill says the tribe follows Levi because, the priesthood being in Levi, the temple where the priests officiated stood in Benjamin or near it, and comes before his elder brother Joseph because his tribe lay between Judah and Joseph. Henry and Wesley add two more: the dignity of Jerusalem, part of which fell in this lot, above Samaria in Ephraim; and Benjamin's adherence to the house of David and the temple when the rest of the tribes deserted both with Jeroboam. Of the title Henry notes that this tribe's father was Jacob's beloved son, the son of his right hand, the tribe being called the beloved of the Lord in allusion to it.

Between his shoulders they read three ways. Clarke takes the shoulders for terrain, within Benjamin's coasts or in his chief city, where the temple was built on Zion and Moriah, here poetically so termed. Ellicott divides the Hebrew so that Jehovah is the one who dwells: beloved of Jehovah, he will dwell in security upon him, covering him all the day, and between his shoulders, his mountain slopes, he hath taken up his abode. Calvin refuses the geography and takes the phrase for a posture: to dwell upon God and between his shoulders is to repose upon him, a similitude taken from fathers who carry their children while they are yet small and tender; and he grants that others extract a different meaning. All find in it the plain fact that God assigned this tribe a dwelling-place in which he in a manner protected them.

That Joseph's blessing is drawn from Jacob's Ellicott makes a general rule, quoting Rashi that in every tribe the blessing of Moses is drawn from the fountain of Jacob's. Calvin says the same more narrowly, that with respect to no other tribe does Moses approach so closely to the patriarch's words, and that although Joseph's family was already divided he begins with the head itself and declares at the close that what was given the fathers pertains to Ephraim and Manasseh; Wesley notes only that in Jacob's blessing Joseph's is the largest, and so here. Keil renders the whole as a catalogue of precious things: of heaven, of the flood beneath, of the produce of the sun and the growth of the moons, of the mountains of old and the everlasting hills. Clarke takes the precious things of heaven for the mildness of the atmosphere and the deep beneath for the water found in digging wells, whence the Septuagint has fountains of the deep; Ellicott quotes Rashi that the deep ascends in vapour and also gives moisture from below.

Of sun and moon Clarke distinguishes crops perfected once a year from vegetables needing about a month, of which several crops may be had; Gill quotes Jarchi that the land of Joseph lay open to the sun, which sweetened its fruits; and Calvin presses the mountains hardest, since their tops are generally uncultivated, or bear only trees without fruit, yet Moses affirms that even there the produce shall be richest. The good will of him that dwelt in the bush Ellicott calls a blessing peculiar to Moses and an exquisite piece of interpretation: from the fact that Jehovah revealed himself in a flame of fire in a bush, the man of God drew the thought that he presented himself as dwelling in it, and so furnished the Church with this comfort for all ages, that his human temple, although it burn with fire, can never be consumed. Clarke draws the same consequence for the persecuted, who shall as surely escape unhurt as the bush, enveloped with fire, was unburnt. Wesley reads the horns of the kingdom Ephraim should obtain under Jeroboam, and Ellicott follows Rashi to the ten thousands slain by Joshua the Ephraimite and the thousands by Gideon of Manasseh.
18:
Zebulun and Issachar are paired for contrast, which Calvin states most fully: two tribes neighbours in position yet very dissimilar, the one devoted to mercantile pursuits and going forth frequently, the other taking more delight in quietude, so that the one is bidden rejoice in its expeditions and the other in its domestic repose. Clarke divides them the same way, prosperity in shipping against prosperity in agriculture and pasturage; Wesley says the course of the one is opposite to the other's, a lover of peace and pasturage; Ellicott sets the warlike character of the first against the more peaceful wisdom of the second. Keil and Gill both note the order, that Moses unites the last two sons of Leah and, like Jacob, places the younger first. Henry adds that their lots made them neighbours, and that Zebulun's going out may be to war, since they jeoparded their lives in the high places of the field, or rather to sea, being a haven of ships.

Whom they call to the mountain divides them squarely. Ellicott keeps it inside Israel, rendering, they shall give the mountain-call to the peoples, that is, shall call the tribes of Israel to Mount Moriah to offer the sacrifices of righteousness. Clarke takes the word the other way, that by their traffic with the Gentiles they should be the instruments of converting many to the true faith, so that instead of sacrificing to idols these would offer sacrifices of righteousness. Wesley agrees and names them, either the men of Galilee, called Galilee of the Gentiles and lying next them, or the nations they traded with, whom they endeavoured to persuade to worship the true God. Gill will have both, that these tribes came up themselves from the distant parts of the land and urged others, Israelites and heathen alike, partly by example and partly by persuasion.

The treasures hid in the sand Clarke calls a difficult passage, and thinks Jonathan ben Uzziel has probably hit the sense in the glass produced from that sand; Keil renders it simply as the hidden treasures of the sand, and Clarke glosses the abundance of the seas as wealth got by merchandise. Of Gad, Clarke reads the enlarging as deliverance out of distress, pointing to the enlargement obtained through Jephthah and to the victories over the Hagarites. Calvin refers the word to the extent of the possession itself, and explains the lion by the position: in that extremity of the land beyond Jordan they were on a hostile border, so Moses declares they would be warlike and compares them to a beast which tears its prey sometimes from the head and sometimes from the arm. Ellicott adds that the mountains of Gilead shut Gad in, and the eleven Gadites whose faces were as the faces of lions.

What the portion of the lawgiver means Ellicott reports and rejects. Rashi interprets it as the field of the lawgiver's burial-place, but this, Ellicott says, can hardly have been in the mind of Moses. Wesley offers two other senses, either that this was the only part of the land Moses was permitted to enter upon, or that it was given by Moses himself, whereas the portions in Canaan were given by Joshua according to the lot. Calvin dismisses Jerome's rendering as quite out of the question and takes the clause to signify that the Gadites were beforehand in seeking a dwelling-place, having asked for Sihon's kingdom before possession of the land was accorded to the people. Gill follows Jarchi in identifying the first part with the land of Sihon and Og, the firstfruits of the subduing of the promised land; Clarke notes that although their portion fell east of Jordan they still went over with the heads of the people to execute the justice of the Lord.
22:
Dan the patriarch compared to a serpent and Moses to a lion, which Henry turns into a question: what could stand before one with the head of a serpent and the heart of a lion? Ellicott keeps the two apart, since the lion of the tribe of Dan is not like the lion of the tribe of Judah, and reads the leap as the taking of Laish, a sudden and treacherous surprise like the spring of a lion on his prey. Calvin will not let the warlikeness pass for a virtue: Dan, like Gad, should be warlike not from disposition but necessity, since their love of war was not praiseworthy, being altogether contrary to humanity, but the unscrupulousness of the enemies that infested them compelled them to arms; and the particle of comparison must be understood, Bashan not lying in this tribe's territory. Clarke reports that the Jewish interpreters make Bashan a haunt of lions, and that Dan's first portion proved insufficient.

Satisfied with favour Wesley makes the point of the whole blessing: it is God's favour, and that only satisfies the soul, so they are happy indeed who have it, and shall have it who place their satisfaction in it; and full with the blessing means not only corn, wine and oil, the fruit, but the blessing itself, the grace of God. Clarke turns the favour toward the gospel, since scarcely any tribe was more favoured, Christ's chief residence having been at Capernaum in this tribe. Keil sets the blessing against Jacob's: where Naphtali's gracefulness was figured by a gazelle, Moses here assures the same tribe of satisfaction with God's favour and promises it the sea and the south. Wesley adds that this last does not describe where his lot actually fell.

Whether Asher is blessed with children or above them is uncertain. Ellicott says the words can be translated, more blessed than all sons, and quotes Rashi's saying that you will not find among all the tribes one so blest with children as Asher, and I cannot say why. Keil renders it, blessed before the sons be Asher, adding that Asher the prosperous justly bore the name. Calvin states the ambiguity outright: the word may mean children, in which case his prolificness is celebrated, or may set up a comparison with the other tribes. Clarke and Wesley both take the children, Clarke wishing him an increasing posterity and Wesley strong and healthful ones, acceptable to his brethren by his sweet disposition, and so supplied with oil that he might wash not only his face in it but his feet. Ellicott closes with a remark of his own, that no tribe has so little recorded of it, and that the happiest lives are sometimes the least eventful.

The shoes of iron and brass Ellicott would not have shoes at all: perhaps we should read, thy bars shall be iron and brass, since the word rendered shoes occurs nowhere else and the nearest means locks or fastenings; and it is uncertain whether the sentence belongs to Asher or to all Israel, though as Asher's territory lay at the northern end of Palestine, close to the pass by which invaders must enter, an assurance about the frontier would be apt. Clarke reads them as armour, since greaves of iron, brass and tin were used by ancient warriors, Goliath having greaves of brass and Homer calling his heroes the brazen-booted Greeks. Gill canvasses three senses: an abundance of the metals such that shoes might have been made of them, as Empedocles is said to have worn shoes of brass; or shoes studded with iron and brass nails, as soldiers use; or, as he thinks truest, the nature of the land itself. Wesley takes the mines plainly; Henry reads the promise that follows as strength proportioned to the day, so that those who have work allotted shall have strength to do it.
26:
That these are the last words Moses ever wrote Henry and Wesley both mark. Henry calls them the last of all that Moses, that great writer, either wrote himself or had written from his dictation, and says that with his last breath he magnifies both the God of Israel and the Israel of God, both incomparable in his eye, his own eye not waxing dim in that judgment; Wesley adds that he was perhaps the greatest writer that ever lived. Calvin sees the movement of the chapter closing here, since Moses proceeds from the parts to the whole and speaks of the body made up of the twelve families, exclaiming in admiration because this inestimable blessing of being protected by God is often but lightly prized. Ellicott sums the verse in words drawn from the song before it, that their rock is not as our Rock.

Jeshurun Clarke will not leave at its literal meaning: the word seems used as an expression of particular affection, so that Calmet understands it as a diminutive of Israel; and he illustrates from the Greek, that sons in the mouth of St John signifies much less than the word properly rendered beloved children, which at once shows the helplessness of the offspring and the tenderness of the parent. Of the eternal God he says the Hebrew means the former God, he who was of old, not like the gods lately come up; and since the arm is the emblem of power in exertion, the everlasting arms declare that an unconquerable power shall be eternally exerted in the defence of God's Church. Keil renders the same clause, abiding is the God of olden time, and beneath are everlasting arms, and rejects a textual alteration proposed on the authority of the ancient versions.

The word for refuge Ellicott and Calvin both trace to one psalm. Ellicott notes that the pronoun thy is not in the original, that the word differs very slightly from the refuge of the ninetieth psalm, also Moses' own, and that the same word is used of the habitation of Jehovah in heaven; he would perhaps join the clause to what precedes and read it as the dwelling of the God of old. Calvin makes the same comparison and draws the comfort out: though the Israelites might be exposed to many injuries, there was secure repose for them under the shadow of God's wings, and unless the hand of God had been like a roof they would have perished a thousand times over. Wesley presses the domestic sense, a habitation or mansion-house in which one is safe and easy and at rest as a man is in his own house, so that every true Israelite is at home in God.

Whether Israel dwelling alone was fulfilled Clarke and Calvin answer oppositely. Clarke says this people shall not be incorporated with any other under heaven, a prophecy which continues to be fulfilled to the very letter, every attempt to unite them with another having proved absolutely ineffectual; Calvin says God never vouchsafed this altogether to them, that they should inhabit their land without fear of enemies, since their ingratitude did not allow of it. Ellicott defers the promise to the days when Judah shall be saved and Israel dwell safely, but not until they learn to rest upon the everlasting arms; Gill takes the safety as confidence, dwelling without fear though surrounded on all hands. Of the enemies found liars Ellicott compares the psalm where they submit themselves, which is literally to lie: the enemies of a conqueror hasten to throw themselves at his feet, protesting they were always his friends, as Shimei did on David's return. Keil insists that saved means not merely delivered from distress but endowed with salvation, and Calvin that this is the only true happiness, since unless we ascend to the first cause all salvations are transitory.
